separate_genres.38192: Separate ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ ବଚନ expression after one Dhaga, inventory separately

comparators.literal_meaning: A son from a well-fed household, yet eager for food!
comparators.explanation: The teasing surprise lies in the mismatch: food is plentiful at home, yet the child lights up at the sight of something to eat. Here ରଙ୍କ carries eagerness for food, rather than the stinginess it carries in another saying on the same dictionary page. Spoken warmly, the line can notice the temptation of a fresh treat even after a meal; spoken sharply, it can embarrass the child. The joke is about that moment, not proof of a child’s character or whether they are hungry.
comparators.cultural_context: The source explicitly describes children in households where food is not lacking. The affectionate scene and discussion of tone are editorial, not observed testimony. Preserve the source’s son wording without making hunger or eagerness a gendered or innate trait. Distinct from 190’s stinginess and 191’s restricted choice.

comparators.odia: ଏଡ଼େ ମଲାଠେଇଁ ଦିଓଳି ବି ତତଲା ଖିଆ!
comparators.literal_meaning: In such dire poverty, yet eating hot food at both meals!
comparators.explanation: The dictionary places this saying under extreme poverty. The line then sets that condition beside eating hot food at both meals: its surprise lies in the contrast. It can be read as a teasing challenge to a description of hardship, though the dictionary does not supply a separate use gloss. Cooking again costs fuel and work; a literary passage about one cooked-rice meal and one meal of pakhala helps explain the image. That context does not make hot food a reliable measure of anyone’s means.
comparators.cultural_context: Recorded as ଢଗ under ମଲା, noun2, printed Praharaj page6322. Preserve the social sting rather than recasting it as a universal lesson about extravagance. The source establishes wording and the poverty sense; the teasing application is editorial. The separate Rudrakshya passage clarifies meal/fuel language but neither quotes nor explains this proverb. No first-use, popularity or community-wide endorsement is claimed.

comparators.odia: ଏତେ ଖାଇ ନ ପୂରିଲା ପେଟ ବିରି ଓଳିଆରେ ମାରୁଛ ହାତ
comparators.literal_meaning: After eating so much, the belly is still not full; you are reaching into the stored black gram.
comparators.explanation: The speaker points out a comic excess: even a substantial meal has not stopped the hand reaching for more. The dictionary places the line under having a full meal; the appetite and the reaching hand are its concrete scene. It can be read as a teasing complaint that someone has already had plenty yet still wants another share. That broader application is an editorial reading, not an additional dictionary gloss. Tone matters: the joke need not be turned into a judgment about a person’s body or genuine hunger.
comparators.cultural_context: The food image is retained as a conversational tease. The source supplies the literal full-meal sense, not a general moral definition. The storage object is retained as ଓଳିଆ in Odia; its construction has not been independently established here.

comparators.odia: କେତେ ଅନଉଛୁ ମତେ, ତୋଠଉଁ ସୁନ୍ଦର ମୋର ବିନୋଦିଆ, ଚାକର ରଖିବ ତତେ
comparators.literal_meaning: Why keep looking at me? My charming one is more beautiful than you and could keep you as a servant.
comparators.explanation: The line answers someone who keeps looking at the speaker by praising another person as more beautiful. The dictionary explains “keep as a servant” here as figurative superiority in wealth or qualities, so the comparison is not a report of employment. One possible performance is a proud rebuff to an admirer: the speaker boasts that a favoured person would far outshine this supposed rival. Neither admiration nor a romantic relationship is fixed by the source gloss, however. The repeated address gives the comparison a personal, theatrical edge. Its status hierarchy is part of the rhetoric, not a measure of anyone’s human worth.
comparators.cultural_context: The source supplies a figurative status comparison, not a named romance or biographical episode. Charming one renders ବିନୋଦିଆ without fixing a romantic relationship; the speaker’s gender and any historical characters are not established. The employment hierarchy should remain visible as rhetoric without being endorsed.

comparators.literal_meaning: The face is beautiful; the body is ugly.
comparators.explanation: The parallel halves divide one person into a praised face and a disparaged body. The dictionary places the last word under “ugly,” not its other senses of a lump or something flat. Our critical reading asks what this splitting does to the person being described. The source supplies the appearance judgment; our objection to reducing someone to it is editorial.
comparators.cultural_context: A short dictionary-labelled expression, not a diagnosis or objective measure of beauty. No gender, body type or community is assigned beyond what the wording establishes.

comparators.odia: ଆଗେରେ କାଳିଆ ! ନାହିଁ କରୁଥିଲୁ ସିଘାଂଣି ନାକକୁ ଦେଖି, ଏବେରେ କାଳିଆ ! ଝୁରି ମରୁଅଛୁ ଥନ ଯଉବନ ଦେଖି
comparators.literal_meaning: Earlier, Kāḷiā, you refused on seeing the runny nose; now, Kāḷiā, you pine away on seeing breasts and youth.
comparators.explanation: The same addressee is called twice, first for rejection and then for longing. The bodily contrast exposes a change in response. Our reading asks what such a reversal reveals about the observer’s standards, rather than treating a person’s worth as dependent on youthful appearance. The source does not identify the speaker, exact ages or relationship.
comparators.cultural_context: The name Kāḷiā is retained without identifying a deity or historical person. The bodily language remains explicit; no life story, universal attraction or documented courtship custom is inferred.

comparators.odia: ପଳେଇ ପଶିଲି ମାଉସୀ ଘରେ ମାଉସୀ ମାଇଲା ଦିପହରେ
comparators.literal_meaning: I fled into my aunt’s house; my aunt struck me at a bad time.
comparators.explanation: The first-person speaker runs towards a relative and meets another blow. Our reading follows that reversal: the hoped-for refuge adds to the trouble. The quotation follows the headword’s “bad time” sense; its other senses are noon and midnight, so a precise clock time is not established here. The line gives one sharp scene, not a verdict on aunts.
comparators.cultural_context: The dictionary’s placement guides this translation without erasing its multiple time senses. The example transfers physical violence into verbal disappointment; it does not approve either.
